title: GraphPipe: Improving Performance and Scalability of DNN Training with Graph Pipeline Parallelism
problem: Existing pipeline-parallel DNN training systems partition models into sequential stages, ignoring the actual DAG topology of modern neural networks, which causes missed model-parallelism opportunities and suboptimal device utilization.
method: GraphPipe introduces graph pipeline parallelism, which partitions a DNN's computation graph (DAG) rather than a linear sequence into pipeline stages. The system represents the DNN as a dataflow graph, identifies parallelizable subgraphs, and maps them to device groups that execute concurrently in a pipeline fashion. A graph-aware scheduling algorithm determines micro-batch execution order across non-linear pipeline stages to maximize throughput and minimize pipeline bubbles, coordinating across branches of the DAG.

title: Rewire: Advancing CGRA Mapping Through a Consolidated Routing Paradigm
problem: Existing CGRA compilers map dataflow graph nodes individually, neglecting inter-node dependencies; this leads to suboptimal placement that misses opportunities to exploit shared routing and structural locality.
method: Generates shareable routing information via propagation across multiple nodes, intersects routing sets to produce individual placement candidates, utilizes data dependencies as constraints to jointly place multiple nodes in one shot rather than individually.

title: Differentiable Net-Moving and Local Congestion Mitigation for Routability-Driven Global Placement
problem: Cell inflation for local congestion mitigation can over-inflate or move cells back into congested areas; global net bounding box minimization may include irrelevant congestion or miss actual bottlenecks; unbalanced placement density degrades pin accessibility.
method: Proposes momentum-based cell inflation tracking historical ratios for local congestion; constructs differentiable global congestion function from Poisson's equation with virtual standard cells on two-pin nets for accurate net movement guidance; adjusts placement density around power/ground rails per congestion patterns.

title: CaMDN: Enhancing Cache Efficiency for Multi-tenant DNNs on Integrated NPUs
problem: Multi-tenant DNN execution on shared SoC NPUs suffers from cache contention that degrades performance; shared cache impact on multi-tenant scenarios not well studied.
method: Architecture-scheduling co-design: lightweight hardware support for model-exclusive cache regions controlled by NPU; cache-aware mapping adapting to varying available capacity; dynamic allocation algorithm adjusting tenant cache usage at runtime.

title: ArbiterQ: Improving QNN Convergency and Accuracy by Applying Personalized Model on Heterogeneous Quantum Devices
problem: In the NISQ era, training and inference on heterogeneous quantum devices is hindered by limited qubits, device noise, and frequent online/offline transitions. Naive distributed QNN approaches destroy accuracy due to device heterogeneity and instability.
method: ArbiterQ applies personalized QNN models for each QPU via two uniform vector representations: model vector (logical-level parameters) and behavioral vector (hardware-level features). By sharing gradients among QPUs with similar behavioral vectors, the framework leverages parallelism while respecting heterogeneity. Additionally, shot-oriented inference scheduling provides fine-grained workload balancing and accuracy optimization.

title: PICACHU: Plug-In CGRA Handling Upcoming Nonlinear Operations in LLMs
problem: Nonlinear operations in LLMs (e.g., softmax, layer norm, GELU, RoPE) contribute significantly to inference latency and are poorly served by fixed-function accelerators designed primarily for matrix multiply/convolution, as they require user-defined precision and flexible dataflow to handle diverse operator shapes and precision requirements.
method: PICACHU uses a Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Array (CGRA) as a plug-in accelerator specifically targeting nonlinear operations in LLMs. The CGRA is configured with reconfigurable processing elements (PEs) arranged in a spatial dataflow grid that can be reprogrammed per operator, supporting user-defined precision via configurable compute units. PICACHU plugs into existing accelerator pipelines (e.g., alongside a systolic array or GPU) and offloads nonlinear operations while the main compute handles linear algebra. The CGRA dataflow is scheduled at compile time per operator using a mapping tool that assigns CGRA PE configurations and routing to match the operator's precision and shape requirements.

title: Dynamic Local Usage: An Accurate Model for Usage of Tile-Internal Wiring in Global Routing
problem: Traditional global routing treats local wiring usage as a pre-estimated constant, ignoring actual wire-shape geometry and packing density, leading to inaccuracies in routing prediction and detailed routing failures.
method: Dynamic Local Usage (DLU) model evaluates wiring usage based on exact wire shapes and specific pin geometries. Introduces tip-to-tip penalty extensions for accurate packing density modeling. New routing algorithms optimize routes according to DLU congestion. Supports incremental changes like pin movements.

title: Affinity-based Optimizations for TFHE on Processing-in-DRAM
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus (TFHE) is a compute- and bandwidth-intensive workload; when mapped to Processing-in-Memory (PIM/HBM) architectures, existing accelerators over-exploit parallelism at the expense of data affinity, causing excessive remote data accesses (RDAs) that degrade performance due to PIM's limited inter-bank communication bandwidth.
method: The paper applies algorithmic optimizations to TFHE to restructure its sub-tasks (bootstrapping, key-switching, NTT/FFT operations) so that data accessed together is co-located on the same PIM vault or bank. An offline scheduler analyzes the affinity patterns of TFHE sub-tasks—determining which operands are used together and how frequently—and derives an optimal scheduling order that minimizes RDAs while maintaining sufficient parallelism. The approach is validated on a variant of an existing PIM-HBM device with minimal hardware modifications and evaluated on a real FPGA-based PIM system emulator.

title: ReaLM: Reliable and Efficient Large Language Model Inference with Statistical Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance
problem: LLM accelerators face hardware faults from aging and variation; existing reliability methods require excessive voltage margins or expensive algorithm-based fault tolerance (ABFT) that ignore LLMs' inherent robustness.
method: ReaLM co-designs circuit and algorithm with statistical ABFT that leverages LLM error tolerance; customizes error detection circuits for online error statistics collection and minimizes error recovery cost.

title: Telos: A Dataflow Accelerator for Sparse Triangular Solver of Partial Differential Equations
problem: Sparse triangular solve (SpTRSV) dominates runtime in preconditioned iterative solvers for PDE-derived linear systems due to loop-carried dependencies that severely limit parallelism. Prior accelerators cannot simultaneously achieve high parallelism and good data locality for structured sparsity from stencil-based PDE discretizations.
method: Telos is a dataflow accelerator that exploits structured (stencil-pattern) sparsity in SpTRSV. A plane-parallel pipelining technique maps dependent computations across processing elements (PEs) while preserving data locality within each plane. A cross-plane communication aggregation technique reorganizes inter-plane data transfers into systolic flows, enabling pipelined resolution of loop-carried dependencies with minimal stall overhead. Computation is overlapped with memory accesses to hide latency.

title: EIGEN: Enabling Efficient 3DIC Interconnect with Heterogeneous Dual-Layer Network-on-Active-Interposer
problem: Chiplet-based 3DIC systems using active interposers struggle with heterogeneous and high-load inter-chiplet network traffic patterns because their interconnects are tightly coupled to top-die designs, preventing flexible topology adaptation and causing high latency and traffic congestion.
method: EIGEN implements a heterogeneous dual-layer interconnect on the active interposer: an application-aware switch-programmable layer (AspLayer) for static topology optimization and a dynamic packet-routing layer (DynLayer) for adaptive traffic management. A reinforcement learning (RL)-based path routing framework is trained with a state space covering topology, network, and memory metrics, with reward defined as the product of average packet latency and link utilization. The two layers cooperate to route inter-chiplet traffic with reduced hops and congestion.

title: PROCA: Programmable Probabilistic Processing Unit Architecture with Accept/Reject Prediction & Multicore Pipelining for Causal Inference
problem: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms for probabilistic programming and causal inference are extremely compute-intensive and inherently sequential, preventing effective parallelization on CPUs and GPUs; existing MCMC accelerators are not programmable across arbitrary posterior distribution forms.
method: PROCA is a programmable MCMC processing unit using processing-in-memory (PIM) function units to generate Markov chain samples. A novel accept/reject prediction methodology predicts whether a proposed sample will be accepted before completing full posterior evaluation, enabling multi-core pipelining: compute for the next sample begins before the current accept/reject decision finalizes. The architecture is programmable to support arbitrary posterior distribution forms compatible with software probabilistic programming frameworks (e.g., PyMC). Implemented using commercial process development kits and validated on 9 benchmarks spanning PyMC tutorials, single-variable problems, and real-world causal inference tasks.

title: ZRAID: Leveraging Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA) for Alleviating Partial Parity Tax in ZNS RAID
problem: ZNS SSD RAID systems must manage partial parity for incomplete stripes; prior approaches log partial parity in reserved zones, creating throughput bottlenecks and exacerbating write amplification that reduces SSD lifetime.
method: ZRAID exploits the Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA), a small random-write buffer region within ZNS SSDs, to buffer and consolidate partial parity in-place before committing full stripes to sequential zones. By using ZRWA as a transient parity staging area, ZRAID avoids persistent partial parity logging to reserved zones, eliminating the associated throughput bottleneck and write amplification. The system coordinates ZRWA usage across multiple ZNS drives to maintain RAID consistency.

title: Topology-Aware Virtualization over Inter-Core Connected Neural Processing Units
problem: Inter-core connected NPUs (e.g., Graphcore IPU, Tenstorrent) require large hardware resources, leading to poor utilization when tasks have imbalanced resource requirements, yet no prior virtualization work accounts for their hardware topology (NoC routing, SRAM-centric cores). Existing MIG-style monolithic virtualization ignores inter-core communication structure and therefore delivers suboptimal performance when multiple workloads share the device.
method: vNPU introduces three integrated techniques: (1) NPU route virtualization redirects instruction and data flow from virtual NPU core IDs to physical cores, constructing a virtual topology over the physical NoC fabric; (2) NPU memory virtualization uses SRAM-centric and NoC-aware address translation to minimize translation stalls and maximize effective memory bandwidth; (3) best-effort topology mapping enumerates candidate virtual topologies and selects the mapping that best balances resource utilization against end-to-end performance for the collocated workload mix. A prototype is validated on FPGA (Chipyard+FireSim) and on a simulator (DCRA).

title: Lincoln: Real-Time 50~100B LLM Inference on Consumer Devices with LPDDR-Interfaced, Compute-Enabled Flash Memory
problem: Consumer devices cannot run large 50-100B LLM models in real time because: (1) Flash storage has insufficient internal read bandwidth for per-iteration weight loading, and (2) the conventional Flash interface (NVMe/UFS) offers far lower transmission bandwidth to the NPU than DRAM interfaces, making both the prefill and decode phases severely bandwidth-limited.
method: Lincoln is a device-architecture co-design with two complementary solutions for the two LLM phases. For the compute-intensive prefill phase, Flash devices use the existing high-speed LPDDR interface (normally used for DRAM) to transmit weights to the NPU at much higher bandwidth than conventional Flash interfaces, while maintaining cost/area efficiency. For the memory-intensive decode phase, hybrid-bonding-based near-Flash computing performs matrix-vector operations directly on Flash dies to exploit the full internal Flash bandwidth without transmission bottlenecks, coupled with speculative decoding to further reduce latency. On the device level, Flash internal bandwidth is increased by improving array shrinking methods (lower read latency, more parallel Flash planes per die), leveraging 3D hybrid bonding already in consumer Flash products.

title: DS-TPU: Dynamical System for on-Device Lifelong Graph Learning with Nonlinear Node Interaction
problem: Electronic Dynamical System (DS) hardware achieves orders-of-magnitude speed and energy improvements over GNNs for graph inference via natural annealing, but it (1) lacks native on-device training support—forcing reliance on slower conventional hardware for model updates—and (2) restricts node interactions to linear functions, limiting expressiveness and training accuracy.
method: DS-TPU introduces two algorithmic-architectural co-design innovations. First, an on-device lifelong learning mechanism uses feedback electric current as a native loss signal in response to observed training data, enabling electron-speed model parameter refinement directly on the DS chip without off-chip software. Second, nonlinear DS node interactions are constructed from Chebyshev polynomial expansions, making the DS hardware compatible with the richer relational structure in graph data while remaining implementable in analog hardware. The DS-TPU architecture is evaluated at a 5-Watt power envelope on six real-world graph learning benchmarks.
